econV54.text021: Robust to weak instruments; may be unbounded
econV54.text023: Anderson-Rubin test curve — invert the test for a robust confidence set
econV54.text026: 2SLS is credible only when the first stage contains a genuine signal. The rule of thumb is F>10; Stock-Yogo critical values offer a stricter standard. Many instruments pull 2SLS back toward OLS bias (bias ≈ ρ·m/F).
econV54.text028: The Anderson-Rubin test of H₀: β=β₀ is equivalent to testing whether y−β₀d is unrelated to Z. It maintains the correct size at any instrument strength. With weak instruments, the confidence set widens or becomes unbounded—an honest reflection of uncertainty.
econV54.text056: Estimator comparison — using only observed outcomes understates or overstates the slope
econV54.text058: When only s=1 observations are observed, E[u|s=1] = ρσ·λ(w'γ) ≠ 0: the inverse Mills ratio λ = φ/Φ is omitted. The two-step method first estimates γ with probit, then adds λ̂ as a regressor in the outcome equation.
econV54.text060: An exclusion restriction z must affect observation without directly affecting y. As γ→0, identification rests solely on the nonlinearity of λ; multicollinearity becomes severe and estimates highly unstable. Move the slider to 0.05 to see this directly.

econV54.text078: Classic ordering in the linear model
econV54.text084: Three test statistics — three geometric views of the same null
econV54.text088: Wald estimates only the unrestricted model and measures how far β̂ lies from the restriction; LM estimates only the restricted model and tests whether the score is zero; LR estimates both and compares fit. They are asymptotically equivalent, with the classic finite-sample ordering W ≥ LR ≥ LM.
econV54.text090: Use LM when the unrestricted model is difficult to estimate, as in nonlinear or constrained models. Use Wald when unrestricted estimation is easy but restrictions are hard to express. Wald is not invariant to reparameterization: equivalent restrictions can produce different conclusions. LR is unaffected.
econV54.text098: Monte Carlo: actual coverage of 95% confidence intervals
econV54.text111: Coverage vs nominal 95% — below the red line signals overconfident inference
econV54.text114: With within-cluster correlation, homoskedastic SEs severely understate uncertainty and coverage collapses. HC1/HC3 address heteroskedasticity, not within-cluster correlation. Cluster-robust inference is asymptotically valid but still understates uncertainty with few clusters. Wild cluster bootstrap-t (Rademacher, imposing H₀) is most reliable when G<15.
econV54.text116: If treatment varies at the cluster level, cluster standard errors at that level. Report wild bootstrap p-values when G < 30.
econV54.text127: y = 0.5 + βx + αᵢ + εᵢₜ; adjustable corr(αᵢ, xᵢₜ)
econV54.text136: H₀: RE is consistent and efficient
econV54.text141: Four estimators and 95% intervals — only FE is robust to correlated individual effects
econV54.text144: Under H₀, RE is consistent and efficient while FE is consistent but less efficient; their difference reflects sampling error alone. Under H₁ (α correlated with x), RE is inconsistent and the difference grows systematically. The statistic is (β̂_FE − β̂_RE)² / (V_FE − V_RE).
econV54.text146: Add group means x̄ᵢ to the RE regression and test whether their coefficients are zero. This is asymptotically equivalent to Hausman and directly accommodates cluster-robust standard errors—a preferred approach in modern empirical work.
econV54.text165: Raw scatter y ~ x₁ (includes the influence of x₂)
econV54.text166: Residualized scatter ỹ ~ x̃₁ (net effect, slope = β̂₁)
econV54.text168: A multiple-regression coefficient equals the simple-regression slope between two sets of residuals after removing all other explanatory variables. This is the same mechanism behind fixed-effects demeaning, two-way fixed-effects DID and partially linear models.
econV54.text170: β̂ remains unbiased, but less residual variation is available, inflating variance by VIF. The remedy is more variation through samples or experimental design, not arbitrary variable deletion.
econV54.text182: y = α·d + X'β + ε, d = X'γ + v (true α = 0.5)
econV54.text201: α̂ comparison — a single LASSO misses confounders that weakly predict y but strongly predict d
econV54.text203: First run LASSO on y to select controls, then run LASSO on treatment d. Take the union of both selections and refit OLS. Inference on α remains approximately valid even with model-selection errors (immunized / Neyman orthogonality).
econV54.text205: Variables with weak effects on y but strong effects on d are dropped by a single LASSO. Their strong association with d amplifies omitted-variable bias. Raise confounding strength to see the blue bar move systematically away from the true value.

econV54.text234: GATES — actual treatment effects by predicted CATE quantile (95% intervals)
econV54.text237: Rank and group observations using out-of-sample CATE predictions, then compare experimental outcomes within each group. Monotonically increasing group effects indicate that the learner captures genuine heterogeneity and can support targeted policy.
econV54.text239: Y ~ a + β₁(D−p̂) + β₂(D−p̂)(τ̂−τ̄). β₁ is the ATE; β₂ is the calibration slope. β₂≈1 means perfect calibration, while β₂≈0 means predictions contain no information. Increase learner noise to reproduce this.

econV55.text047: p-values use MacKinnon (1996) response-surface approximations (ADF/PP/DF-GLS) and quantile interpolation from Kwiatkowski et al. (1992) (KPSS; boundary values shown outside [0.01, 0.10]). ADF critical values use the MacKinnon finite-sample response surface cv(T) = cv∞ + a/T + b/T².
econV55.text058: ADF/PP/DF-GLS test the null of a unit root; KPSS tests stationarity. Two of the four combinations indicate insufficient evidence—an accurate description of short samples and near-unit-root regions. Do not repeatedly change deterministic terms to engineer a preferred conclusion.
econV55.text060: DF-GLS has materially greater power than ADF near ρ→1. Breaks make conventional ADF tests seriously understate stationarity, requiring Zivot-Andrews. ADF alone cannot detect the seasonal unit roots in (1−L⁴) for quarterly data.

econV55.text066: ACF cuts off at lag one

econV55.text081: All MA roots outside the unit circle
econV55.text091: Wold coefficients ψⱼ — propagation of a single shock
econV55.text092: Characteristic roots and the unit circle
econV55.text100: Any zero-mean, covariance-stationary, purely nondeterministic process can be written as yₜ = Σψⱼεₜ₋ⱼ. This describes second-order structure and linear projection; it does not imply that the economic mechanism is linear, nor that εₜ is automatically a structural shock.
econV55.text102: The PACF cutoff at p for AR(p) and ACF cutoff at q for MA(q) require stationarity, linearity, no breaks and a sufficiently large sample. Slowly decaying sample ACFs near a unit root do not imply high-order AR dynamics. Information criteria provide limited evidence, not a substitute for institutional context and research objectives.
econV55.text124: Spurious regression: |t| distribution from regressing two independent random walks
econV55.text126: The cost of overdifferencing (the data are stationary AR(1))
econV55.text133: Trend stationary vs difference stationary: two extrapolations of the same series
econV55.text138: Differencing log levels changes the question from how the price level responds to how inflation responds. Overdifferencing a trend-stationary series introduces an MA root near −1, amplifies forecast errors and discards long-run information.
econV55.text140: Under trend stationarity, forecast interval width approaches a constant; under a unit root, it diverges at √h. These give entirely different answers about whether a shock is permanent, yet short samples often cannot distinguish them. Report results from both approaches in that case.

econV55.text166: ; γ→∞ reduces to the hard switching of SETAR.
econV55.text172: Threshold c is identified only under nonlinearity, so the standard F distribution does not apply. The Hansen (1996) bootstrap repeatedly generates data under the linear null to obtain the empirical supF distribution. That is how the p-value here is computed.
econV55.text174: Threshold models capture state dependence: persistence may be far higher in recessions than expansions, and arbitrage may begin only when deviations exceed transaction costs. Linear AR averages both regimes into an intermediate parameter, systematically understating dynamics in extreme states.
econV55.text195: Selecting break count: SSR / BIC / LWZ
econV55.text206: Exhaustive search over m breaks costs O(Tᵐ). Bai-Perron (1998, 2003) use dynamic programming over segment SSRs to reduce this to O(T²), allowing joint estimation of break locations and counts.
econV55.text207: Treat stability as a testable hypothesis:
econV55.text208: Estimating one set of stable parameters over the full sample is a common implicit assumption. Break tests make that assumption explicit: a single crisis or policy-regime shift can turn full-sample estimates into a meaningless average.
econV55.text229: Scorecard: log score / CRPS / PIT uniformity / coverage / pinball
econV55.text234: PIT histogram — a well-calibrated density should be close to uniform (10%)
econV55.text238: Risk management concerns the entire conditional distribution. PIT = F̂ₜ(yₜ) is uniform under a correctly specified density. A U-shaped histogram indicates intervals that are too narrow (understated risk); an inverted U indicates intervals that are too wide.
econV55.text240: Log scores and CRPS are strictly proper scoring rules: honestly reporting the true density is optimal. CRPS belongs to the pinball-loss family and weights the entire distribution, making it more robust than checking VaR hit rates alone.
econV55.text276: Pairwise DM tests across M models create a serious multiple-comparison problem. The model confidence set of Hansen, Lunde and Nason (2011) uses sequential equivalence tests and bootstrap distributions to produce a set containing the best model with probability 1−α. Not identifying a single winner is itself informative.
econV55.text278: The forecast combination puzzle: equal-weight combinations often beat any single model and estimated optimal weights, because weight-estimation error is costly in small samples.
econV55.text303: GARCH specifies conditional variance as a deterministic function of past observations, allowing the likelihood to be written directly. SV treats log volatility as a latent state, requiring integration over the entire state path. Here a bootstrap particle filter approximates that integral, and likelihood is maximized over a (φ, σ_η) grid.
econV55.text305: SV models volatility shocks more flexibly and connects naturally to continuous-time stochastic volatility models such as Heston, but estimation is expensive (MCMC / particle MCMC). GARCH is cheap to estimate and often holds its own out of sample, making it a practical default for risk management.
